The Geekom A5 2027 Edition represents solid value for the indie generalist seeking out a compact form factor

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamesradar

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Geekom A5 2027 won't replace a Steam Machine, but it's not designed to.
  • Upgradeable RAM and SSD via easily accessible bays.
  • Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Geekom A5 2027 won't replace a Steam Machine, but it's not designed to. This is an efficiency-focused productivity cube designed to see you through more casual workflows without breaking a sweat or pulling too much power. That means it won't zipping through Cyberpunk, but its handling of lighter indie and retro titles is still impressive.

Upgradeable RAM and SSD via easily accessible bays.

Chipset prioritizes efficiency over power.

Some ports slightly too close together.

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

The Geekom A5 2027 doesn't want to be the answer to your Steam Machine woes. I've been road testing the mini PC with a gaming mindset but, in truth, this is productivity focused device that just so happens to handle indie and retro titles particularly well.

Recent findings suggest that with current PC prices ravaging the industry, and no signs of those inflated rates slowing down, anyone on the hunt for a day to day productivity machine will be keen to double up on their purchase. With prices sitting well below the rest of the PC gaming market ($549 / £469 for the configuration on my desk), the Geekom A5 2027 has an interesting proposition for those with an indie-focused Steam library.

In a recent development, the latest in a line of budget-friendly mini PCs, the 2027-monikered device refreshes its chip with an AMD Ryzen 7 7730U, while also offering expandable memory and storage. That's all wrapped up in a compact, sturdy brick of a chassis with plenty of ports for all your day to day connections.

3x USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A, 2x USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, 1x USB 2.0 Type-A, 2x HDMI 2.0, 1x 3.5mm audio, 1x 2.5G RJ45, 1x SD card reader.

The good thing about mini PCs is it's pretty difficult to make one that looks cheap. There are so few materials compared to the best gaming PCs on the market, higher quality builds are far more accessible at lower prices.

Recent findings suggest that the Geekom A5 2027 falls into the same aesthetic step as its counterparts across the market, as well as its predecessors. This is a compact silver block with a tiny footprint on the desk. There's an extra air of luxury in those shiny metallic accents running around the perimeter, though, with a sturdy slightly mottled silver in the main casing.

Heat is mostly dispensed through vents to the rear, sitting above a set of fully labelled ports, with intake grills lining each side of the device. The bottom panel plays host to four user-removable screws, providing access to upgradeable SSD and memory bays with handy orientation information stamped into the plastic. Four rubberized feet house these screws, keeping the PC firmly in place on the desk.

Those after a mini PC for its portability will also be glad to see the tiny power adapter included. This power block is dwarfed by the units I often have to wrangle when testing the best gaming laptops, and makes for lightweight, easy backpack transport.

Geekom has outfitted the A5 2027 Edition with AMD's Ryzen 7 7730U chipset, alongside a cheaper Ryzen 5 7430U option. Configurations keep things conservative, with 16GB DDR4 RAM and 512GB SSDs dominating most listings (some are available with 256GB or 1TB SSD sticks).

That processor tells us a lot about what Geekom wants you to be doing with its mini PC, though. The Ryzen 7 5825U refresh includes an integrated GPU, but it's not the Radeon 780M you'll find in a lot of gaming-focused mini PCs.

Sources indicate that this is an octacore chip with 16 threads for lightweight but efficient processing, relying on a TDP of just 15W. Its use in slimline laptops over the years has given it plenty of time in the sun, but packaging it into a 2027-branded mini PC means Geekom is pitching its latest iteration as a power-efficient everyday productivity machine.

This isn't a rig designed to take on your Steam library, but it can certainly give lighter titles a go.

Recent findings suggest that using slower DDR4 RAM is going to take some of the sheen off if you're running more demanding workloads, though it is upgradeable to 64GB with a handy socketed design. That generational step down from DDR5 to DDR4 isn't going to be felt too keenly by most casual everyday uses, though. Under the hood, you'll also find space for two swappable NVMe SSDs, as well as a miniature SATA.

Ports remain plentiful as well. The front houses two USB-As with a 3.5mm audio out for easy access, all lined up in step with that glowing power button. The left panel holds that full-sized SD card reader. Two additional USB-As are at the rear, alongside two USB-Cs, two HDMI 2.0, an RJ45 and the power connection.

That's enough for a good selection of accessories, though I was a little frustrated that the two rear USB-A ports are aligned a little too close together. Chunkier cable connections struggle to sit on top of each other here, effectively rendering one of those ports redundant.

This is a cheaper iteration so there's no USB4 standard on the USB-Cs.

Industry observers note that the Geekom A5 2027 Edition has been designed to confidently deliver seamless day to day productivity without breaking the bank, and this is where it excels. My workflow typically requires far too many Chrome tabs, separated in a splitscreen window, with image editing software and Spotify running in the background. The A5 barely broke a sweat.

Industry observers note that curiosity got the better of me when it came to testing the Geekom A5 2027's gaming performance, though. This is in no way a machine Geekom expects you to buy for its raw power, so my Cyberpunk 2077 tests are to be taken as an indication of upper limits rather than a condemnation of the product itself. Starting things off a little easier, though, I was glad to see those internals keeping up with lighter indie games particularly well.

I could have been playing on a far more expensive machine when I booted up Stardew Valley and Islanders. Both titles ran smoothly, with no jagged edges, obviously dropped frames, or stutters - even when wildly panning around my poorly planned civilizations in the latter. Low-weight indies are this machine's bread and butter - if that's all you play, there's no reason to spend above the Geekom's price tag.

More demanding games are runnable but not entirely enjoyable.

Shadow of the Tomb Raider represents the mid-size titles that might have been in your Steam library for the last five to ten years. Games that don't stress too many GPUs in this day and age, but still represent a sizeable jump from lightweight indie titles.

It has been revealed that to stay above 30fps here, we have to drop things down to their lowest possible settings - at 720p resolution. That's the point where Tomb Raider feels smooth enough to relax into, rather than constantly watching for dips, though there's a sizeable amount of visual sacrifice to be made at these settings. Still, it's playable and considering current PC prices I'll still take that as a win from a machine not typically designed for such outings.

Then I switched over to Cyberpunk, for science purposes.

Sources indicate that to stay comfortably above at 30fps threshold for a lighter machine, the Geekom A5 2027 edition needs to be running on Low settings at 720p with frame generation on. Again, tests prove it runs - but it's going to be spicy.

Recent findings suggest that CPU tests show what we expect from this older efficiency-focused chipset. The AMD Ryzen 7 7730U falls behind the faster, flashier AMD AI 9 HX 470 inside the Geekom A9 Max's 16,993 multi-core score and 2,740 single-core score. That's a machine that costs three times the A5's price, though.

According to recent reports, the story's much the same in 3D Mark. The Geekom A5 2027 didn't expect to be put through these benchmarks as a budget-minded productivity-focused device, but for the sake of comparison across the price range, here's how it fared.

The Geekom A5 2027 is perfectly suited to those looking for a lightweight everyday computing brick that can keep the party going with lighter indie titles after work. The mini PC's focus on cooling and efficiency makes for a sustainable performance across less demanding tasks that makes it ideal for those smaller entries in your Steam library and emulation alike.

Industry observers note that if you're just looking for an indie runner, and have no need for a full Windows PC attached to it, the price gets a little squeakier. While it's nice having that full Windows compatibility to back you up, especially if you're looking to build a retro library, those just looking to play the indies they like may fare better with a console.

Still, for day to day workflow with room for upgradeability and nicely quiet operation, this is an easy recommendation.

I used the Geekom A5 2027 Edition as my daily driver for work across two weeks, while using it for all my indie gaming during the same period. The A5 was put through its paces in Stardew Valley and Islanders, while also being specifically benchmarked across Shadow of the Tomb Raider, Cyberpunk 2077, 3D Mark's Time Spy, Fire Strike and Steel Nomad Lite, and Geekbench 7. Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: There were 47 graphics chip makers in 1998. Where did they all go?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price.
  • In 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves.
  • It has been revealed that but the Nvidia of the late 1990s and early 2000s was a far cry from the vast (if tarnished) juggernaut it is today, and at the time it wasn’t even the obvious survivor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price. It was choosing the right one among a glut of potential, reasonably affordable options.

In 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves. Just two years later, at the turn of the new millennium, only 15 remained, and not long after that, there were merely two: Nvidia and ATI, nowadays part of AMD.

It has been revealed that but the Nvidia of the late 1990s and early 2000s was a far cry from the vast (if tarnished) juggernaut it is today, and at the time it wasn’t even the obvious survivor. Research firm 4th Wave put ATI top for 1998 with 24.5 million 3D chips sold, followed by S3 with 15.2 million and Intel, in its first year in the market, with 6.5 million. Nvidia came fourth on 6.4 million. 3dfx, the company whose Voodoo cards had made 3D gaming on PC a thing in the first place, sold 5.2 million.

Each of those companies went under or sold up for one reason or another, but what’s striking is how most did so within a few years of one another. In the four years between 1998 and 2002, the graphics business essentially stopped rewarding whoever had the fastest chip, instead favouring the companies that could iterate the fastest. A new chip every six months or so for the same APIs everyone used, backed by enough capital to ride out the dot-com crash. Nvidia was built for that; almost nobody else was.

Sources indicate that the first companies to go didn’t need any help from Nvidia, though. 3D acceleration had made the humble graphics chip a much bigger and more expensive thing to design, and plenty of incumbents that had found their footing on 2D couldn’t afford to keep going. Tseng Labs stopped developing graphics chips at the end of 1997 with roughly $28 million still in the bank, selling its graphics engineers to ATI for about $3 million. Rendition, maker of the Vérité V1000 3D accelerator, agreed to sell itself to memory maker Micron in June 1998, and ATI bought Chromatic Research for $67 million that October.

Recent findings suggest that in its prospectus for its January 1999 IPO, Nvidia warned that PC makers brought out newly introduced systems as often as twice a year, on a spring and fall schedule, and that missing one was a serious risk. The company subsequently reorganised itself around that schedule, releasing the GeForce 256 in October 1999 and the GeForce 3 in February 2001. By 2002, Nvidia’s annual report disclosed that separate design teams were working on several generations of chips at once.

By this point, though, the writing had been on the wall for quite some time. S3, then the world’s second-largest graphics chip maker, wrote in its annual report for 1999 that a graphics chip stayed on sale for 12 to 18 months, and that a delay "as short as a few months" could cost it a design win with a PC maker. Any organization that was rolling out just one major chip per year was launching against a rival’s refresh at best. At worst, it was launching late against next-gen chips.

That’s essentially what happened to 3dfx when Rampage, the chip that was meant to succeed the Voodoo5, never shipped. The firm lost its other big advantage around the same time with Glide, its own programming interface that only ran on Voodoo cards. Glide flourished while Direct3D, Microsoft’s rival interface built into Windows, was still lacking features, meaning that plenty of games ran best on 3dfx hardware, but that lead was promptly eroded once Direct3D and rivals’ OpenGL drivers caught up; developers could now write a game once and run it on anyone’s card. By 1999, Creative was selling Nvidia-based Riva TNT cards with drivers that let Glide games run on them. 3dfx sued, then open-sourced Glide altogether that December.

Industry observers note that by then, though, 3dfx had already made its most damaging mistake. A year earlier, on December 14, 1998, it agreed to buy graphics card maker STB Systems for about $141 million in stock, and CEO Greg Ballard noted the Voodoo3 would only be sold on 3dfx’s cards. That revelation left Diamond and Creative in a tough spot, having built their gaming lines on Voodoo chips. They were now stuck high and dry without access to the fresh one.

Recent findings suggest that 3dfx was solely concerned with its margins here. The price of its single-chip Voodoo Banshee card dropped from $150 to $89 within a month of launch. With prices in freefall, selling the finished Voodoo Banshee meant that 3dfx pocketed the margin that’d otherwise go to a partner like Diamond or Creative. Those boardmakers inevitably walked, and went where the chips were. STB had been selling Nvidia cards right up to the deal, and its last annual report includes a $3 million note it held from "Nvidia Corporation, a supplier." Creative already had Riva TNT cards on shelves, and Nvidia, which then didn’t make its own cards, would sell its chips to anyone.

Recent findings suggest that intel, meanwhile, was causing problems from the other end of the market. Its i740 "Auburn" graphics chip released in early 1998, and Microprocessor Report, the newsletter for the industry’s engineers, argued that Intel’s arrival encouraged Cirrus Logic, Oak and others to fold that year. Just over a year later, after lacklustre sales, Intel confirmed that it was ending support for the i740, then pulled out of standalone desktop graphics chips altogether to put graphics into its motherboard chipsets instead, starting with the i810. This was extremely problematic for companies like S3, Trident, and SiS. They survived on cheap chips for massive PC makers, and by the second half of 2001, estimates say Intel’s integrated graphics business had risen to control 55% of the market. That, in turn, pushed S3 to sell its graphics business to a VIA joint venture for $323 million.

In a recent development, then the money ran out. Venture funding for graphics startups had already dried up in 1999 as the dot-com bubble deflated, and exits inevitably followed. 3dfx lost $100.5 million in the second quarter of 2000, with its CEO blaming a late Voodoo5, and on December 15 that year it sold its assets to Nvidia for $70 million in cash (and a million Nvidia shares) after failing to secure credit. STMicroelectronics, which made the PowerVR-based Kyro II, quit PC graphics in early 2002.

Recent findings suggest that ATI, however, survived alongside Nvidia because it was already operating in the way the latest market wanted it to. It was the biggest seller at the time, and it made its own graphics cards, which Microprocessor Report stated brought in most of its revenue and margin. So, making its own cards wasn’t 3dfx’s mistake; it was locking out boardmakers who had been selling Voodoo cards for it. That pushed those boardmakers towards Nvidia, and a late Voodoo5 and cash crunch dealt the death blow. ATI also used its stock to buy the engineers that its rivals were shedding: Tseng’s, Chromatic’s, then, in February 2000, ArtX’s for $400 million, a team that’d just designed the Flipper graphics chip for Nintendo’s GameCube.

Sources indicate that for the next two decades, the the graphics industry was dominated by ATI - which eventually folded into AMD in 2006 - and Nvidia. For a while, it was a real fight. AMD paid $5.4 billion for ATI, and in the second quarter of 2010, Radeon cards briefly overtook Nvidia in discrete graphics shipments. However, AMD had a problem: it couldn’t really afford ATI. It wrote off $1.6 billion of goodwill from the deal about a year after it closed, and its PC chip business kept struggling.

By early 2015, AMD’s CPU and GPU revenue was down 38% on the year, and the tech giant was close to negative book value. Its quarterly R&D budget had fallen to its lowest level since 2004, with Nvidia spending nearly half as much again. Radeon cards stayed on the same Graphics Core Next architecture for about seven years before RDNA arrived in 2019. By then, Nvidia had already released its RTX cards with dedicated ray tracing hardware and Tensor cores for AI, and it never gave that lead back.

In a recent development, intel was the only company with pockets deep enough to try breaking back in. Its first go, Larrabee, was cancelled as a consumer graphics chip in December 2009. It finally got there in 2022, when the Arc A770 went on sale from $329, alongside the cheaper A750. Both arrived after repeated delays and struggled with older DirectX 9 games, and many observers - RPS included - put their chances of breaking up the Nvidia-AMD duopoly at low. By the time then-hardware editor James returned to the A750 in 2023, Intel had drastically improved its drivers, bringing massive gains to both general performance and DX9 compatibility. Even then, the Arc series had yet to prove it could work well at launch, without the need to be ironed out across months of updates.

It has been revealed that the second generation did indeed fare better, with the Arc B580 successfully selling out at $249 in December 2024. But that still barely impacted the wider industry, with Intel sitting at just 1% of graphics card shipments in the third quarter of 2025 and around 2% this spring, when Nvidia took roughly 90% of the 12.5 million cards shipped.

It now looks like Intel is on its way back out of gaming graphics cards. In April, leaker Jaykihn claimed that its next-generation Celestial gaming cards had been cancelled "long ago," and the latest rumours say B580 supply could be cut so Intel can sell more Arc Pro cards for, surprise surprise, AI work. It’s important to note that Intel hasn’t confirmed any of that, and one of its execs has remarked that Arc isn’t leaving its PC roadmap. Still, Intel had everything 3dfx didn’t: the cash, the PC makers on side, and the same APIs as everyone else. But money can’t buy two decades of Nvidia and AMD fixing their drivers game by game, and it seems to have decided its capital is better spent on AI anyway.

Evidently, the question of where all the other GPU makers went does not have one single answer. Some couldn’t afford the rising costs, some couldn’t keep pace with a new Nvidia chip every six months, and some lost their cheap business to Intel’s integrated graphics or went under when the dot-com bubble burst. Left over was a Nvidia/ATI (later AMD) duopoly, and PC gamers haven’t exactly done well out of it. We saw the RTX 4080 launch at $1,199 in 2022, nearly twice the 3080’s price, and the ongoing, AI-driven RAM shortage has pushed prices higher still.

Industry observers note that in 1998, 47 companies wanted your money. Now there are two, and the bigger one, Nvidia, sells nine of every 10 graphics cards - yet still makes most of its money from data centres. Eighteen years on, it's a bad time to be a PC gamer, and nobody’s in a hurry to make things any better.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HoYoverse just wrapped up a pretty exciting Zenless Zone Zero Special Program that not only delivered all the details on the next big update, it also came with the unexpected announcement that the action RPG is on its way to Steam.

It has been revealed that previously, all HoYoverse games with PC versions have always been directly available from the developer’s website, or through the Epic Games Store. In other words, Zenless Zone Zero will soon mark the massive firm’s debut on Valve’s platform.

Recent findings suggest that the main focus of the livestream, of course, has been Version 2.8, otherwise known as New Eridan Sunset. This upcoming release is scheduled for May 6, though the Steam version does not yet have a date.The new release sees the release of two new Agents, as well as the brand-new Wind attribute enemy.

Sources indicate that the release also acts as the last chapter of Season 2, and it sees Ramiel becoming the main target of different factions in the Outer Ring. The two fresh arrivals, together with Proxies and Cissia will embark on a quest to learn the new identity of Ramiel.

According to recent reports, the first new Agent is Promeia, the executioner of Krampus. She’s an S-Rank Ice Anomaly Agent who can consume Trial by Cold to trigger Abloom on enemies. This is done by converting Corrosive Chill.

It has been revealed that by using her EX Special Attack, she can enter the Bound Absolution state, which allows her to automatically Perfect Dodge any attack that targets her. If you have another Anomaly or Support Agent on the team, Promeia can further boost the entire squad’s Abloom damage.

The second addition in 2.8 is Starlight - Billy, also an S-Rank Agent, though wielding Physical Rupture instead. This is the upgraded form of Billy, and he arrives on a combat motorcycle to bring his signature Starlight Knight to the fight. Through it, he can deliver big Physical burst damage.

The higher Billy’s health, the more Sheer damage he deals. In fact, all Physical damage he deals lands as Sheer damage. Further building on his tank-like role, his skills can also restore his own health.

Sources indicate that re-runs in Version 2.8 will be Lucia in the first half, and Orphie & Magus in the second. The other exciting addition coming with this upgrade is the new Wind attribute enemy, and the accompanying Vortex mechanic.

Sources indicate that when an enemy is inflicted with the Wind Attribute Anomaly, any other Anomaly attack type that gets applied will trigger Vortex, rather than Disorder. This deals AoE Anomaly damage of the type that matches the corresponding element.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the version’s runtime, you’ll be able to take part in the Marcel Bootopia-themed event, which gives you control of Eous and lets you explore a Bangboo resort island. The island has been closed due to an outbreak of Hollows, and you must rescue Bangboos and find treasures.

Recent findings suggest that if you do, you’ll earn Booltergeist and its Bangboo core for your troubles. This is an A-Rank Bangboo that can float around and fire lasers in combat. Its damage is further boosted whenever certain teammates are present.

In a recent development, the Ultimate Verdict Trial is another event you can check out that lets you fight alongside newcomer Promeia, or take part in other mini-activities that all reward Polychrome. Finally, you can look forward to a newly introduced Hoshimi Miyabi outfit: Dignified Blossom, which will be available in the store.

Before you jump back in next month, it always helps to catch up on the latest Zenless Zone Zero codes to make sure you’re not missing out on any freebies.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has been a huge success for Nintendo, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game ever, shifting more than 5.2 million copies in four days.

Nintendo announced the sales result this morning in a press release, specifying that the record relates only to Nintendo-published games. But since Nintendo's games are the most popular Switch 2 games, the fastest-selling-ever title presumably holds.

Recent findings suggest that it's an incredible result for a game that's been received with enormous enthusiasm. Christian Donlan awarded The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time five golden stars in Eurogamer's review, saying: "Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve." We've also already seen a jump in US Switch 2 sales because of the game's release. So much for not launching in November near GTA 6, eh?

This level of success begs the question of whether Nintendo would consider remaking more beloved old Zelda games - or Nintendo games - to replicate this nostalgia-driven effect. Are there other Zelda games that have the pull of Ocarina of Time that haven't been remade or remastered already in some capacity?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that having to refuel cars in GTA 6 was weirdly one of the most talked about features before launch—I guess people didn't like the idea of having to pull over for gas while being chased by half the Vice City's police department. But the reality is that refuelling cars is something you'll barely find yourself doing.

When your ride does run low on fuel, you can find a gas station on the map via the gas pump symbols:.

Industry observers note that easy, right? And you'll barely have to do it since, just like real life, cars can go quite a long time without refuelling if they have a full tank, even if you're going over 60mph, which I assume you are. Note that if you steal a stranger's car, their tank may nearly be empty already.

It has been revealed that if you're driving an electric car, check the map for recharging stations. Pull up close to one, select "Charge Vehicle," and it'll display the cost. You'll see a quick scene of the readout on the charging station filling the battery to 100%, and when it's done, you can drive away.

In a recent development, now, the better reason to visit Vice City's fuel stations is that they can repair your vehicle, and if you drive like I do, you'll need this a lot. This is a separate interaction at the same gas pump: on the"Services" menu, just select "Repair" instead. The camera will whoosh into the sky for a moment, and when it returns to ground level your ride will be fixed.

The cost depends on how much damage you've done to your vehicle, but it's well worth it if you want to retain your ride, considering the usual vehicular wear-and-tear that comes with being a professional criminal.

Since you can customise your beloved vehicles at the Mod Shop, or even claim fancier cars by removing their trackers at the Pay 'n' Spray, once you unlock this in the story, keeping your car in good condition is a worthwhile investment.

Minerva Rising is a post-apocalyptic city builder in which your city extends deep underground, divided into levels with their own resources, industries, and communities. You are an artificial intelligence with overall control, but watch out: if you alienate the population of any particular level by, say, forgetting to supply them with oxygen, subversives may rise up and cut your feed, blinding you to their activities.

I'm keen to know whether it's possible for every level to lose faith in you and hack your cameras, reducing the game to a pile of "SIGNAL NOT FOUND" messages. I'm also imagining turning the feeds back on and discovering that everybody is having a massive orgy. Stupid sexy vault dwellers! You'll go forth and multiply when Deep Thought tells you to, and not a second before.

Who needs the sun? Can't get sunburn from a glowing mushroom, can you? Look, citizens of level 13: you'd better overcome your distaste for giant toadstools or I'm turning the power off again. Damn it, you stay the hell away from my factory reset button. "WELCOME TO MICROSOFT WINDOWS 95." Balls! "[✓] SHOW THIS WELCOME SCREEN NEXT TIME YOU START WINDOWS." Right, that's it. I don't appear to have any military options in this game, but I'm pretty sure I can redesignate your whole cave as a compost heap.

"Cut through newly introduced strata of earth and ethics each playthrough," the Steam page enthuses. "No two games will be the same. One run might face blight and starvation, while another might be low on coal for producing power. Your decisions and the resources you find provide different challenges each time you play. Even if your people live to see the sun again, there are varied and sundry ways to get there." There's no release date for it yet. If you'd rather build cities in the other direction, check out Stario: Haven Tower.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hoYoverse just wrapped up a new Genshin Impact Special Program, where the developer revealed everything there is to know about the game’s next major update. Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana, or as its friends call it, Luna 7, was unveiled as part of the showcase.

This next update has a lot going for it, and it will be in players’ hands everywhere on May 20.

Industry observers note that luna 7 will take us back to Sumeru for its new Archon Quest, where a new crisis that threatens to plunge the nation into chaos is brewing. Nahida is out of the picture, and someone who looks suspiciously like Il Dottore has emerged.

Sources indicate that if you complete this chapter at launch, you’ll earn up to 560 Primogems, as well as Nicole's Ascension Materials. Nicole is the first of three playable characters arriving with this patch. Something else you’ll unlock if you finish the chapter quickly is a latest Weekly Boss that HoYo claims has “unpredictable abilities.”.

And if you haven’t played in a while, don’t worry, you can refer to the Guiding Notes feature to catch you up on what’s been going on in the world. This is part of a larger effort from the team to make story progression more seamless, and also includes improved quest autosave prompts.

Nicole Reeyn is highest-profile and most interesting, being the first playable member of the Hexenzirkel. The mage is a 5-Star Pyro Catalyst wielder intended as a support member of the team. She can boost the ATK of all party members, even those not currently on the field. She also generates a shield while doing so.

According to recent reports, her Elemental Burst allows her to summon an Arcane Projection that follows the active character, sending out Coordinated Attacks that match their Elemental Type. Outside of combat, Nicole can help you find treasures by calling upon a Seelie to guide you to them. Quite fitting, as you’ll be exploring in the inside of the Witch's Lodge in Nicole’s Meeting Point in Luna 7, so bring her along.

Industry observers note that lohen, the Vice Captain of the Knights of Favonius' Fifth Tech giant, is the second latest character. Also a 5-Star addition, he is instead a Cryo Polearm wielder designed for aggressive combat. His main use is dealing massive Cryo DMG, and he can do that by managing two resources unique to him: Joy, and Will to Win.

Through his Elemental Skill, he can enter the Masterstroke state, allowing him to build up (and consume) Joy to unleash enhanced skills. The more his teammates fight, the more Will to Win he biulds, which can later be used to boost his effectiveness further. For an even more powerful display of force, bring along a Hexerei character when he’s on your team.

According to recent reports, prune is the third and final addition. Prune is a 4-Star Anemo Catalyst wielder, and her kit is inspired by her Witch Hunter aspirations. Using a bell and a hammer, she can deal DMG of several elements at once, and trigger Swirl reactions.

Nicole, and Lohen will debut in Luna 7’s first half, while Prune will follow in the second. The first half will also see a Durin rerun, with Mavuika returning in the second half. You can look forward to a new limited-time event as part of Luna 7, with a focus on Klee's Little Hexenzirkel.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll find a series of mini-games you can play alongside Prune, as well as Qiqi, Yaoyao, and Sayu. If you play, you could earn the Super Awesome Magic Key, an exclusive weapon skin. Miliastra Wonderland is doing its thing, too, with a upcoming sports festival for you to take part in.

According to recent reports, one newly introduced gameplay addition worth calling attention to is that Manekins can now perform actions in Teyvat. The Kamera, which you can use to capture moments with Manekins, is getting upgraded, too, with new editing tools and assets.

Before you pick the game back up, be sure to check out our recently-updated Genshin Impact codes page for some free stuff you may be missing.

On PS5 Pro, that 30fps is supposed to be "unwavering". The report describes performance as "exceptionally robust" with "perfect frame pacing" — meaning that the game feels super responsive despite its 30fps cap.

But to be clear, it's not like GTA 6 is a mess on the base PS5 — it just comes with some drawbacks.

In a recent development, alongside the aforementioned downgrade in visual clarity, the game struggles to maintain a solid 30fps at times. The frame rate holds up fine during general gameplay, but it looks like busier scenarios start to drag it down.

You can get "minor dips" when driving at speed, with more "sustained" drops occurring when you're partaking in especially hectic combat encounters, complete with explosions.

These bigger bouts of choppiness can reportedly see the frame rate drop down into the mid-20s, which is obviously far from unplayable, but it's certainly not ideal.

But again, Digital Foundry makes it clear that Rockstar had to compromise on overall performance to deliver on its ridiculously ambitious open world vision — which falls in line with what the developer told us here at Push Square.

Indeed, the analysis heaps praise on the game's borderline photorealistic lighting, and "arguably the best implementation of ray tracing we've seen to date".   • Back in July, Doom developers id Software laid off around a hundred people as part of wider Microsoft blood-letting.
  • Hidden Horses have 20 id Software alumni on the books, including former lead VFX artist Todd Boyce, principal engine programmer Dustin Land, senior AI and gameplay engineer Daniel Young, producer Andrew Willis, senior technical designer Jordan Turner, principal technical designer Tim Locke, and senior skybox artist Allison Dombek.
  • In a recent development, all members of Hidden Horses own a share of the manufacturer, with bosses "democratically" appointed, in the words of a FAQ.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in July, Doom developers id Software laid off around a hundred people as part of wider Microsoft blood-letting. Now, a few of those devs have founded a new employee-owned studio, Hidden Horses. Their first project is Danger Pay, a single-player FPS influenced by ancient arcade blaster Smash TV (pictured) and dystopian movies such as deadly gameshow fable The Running Man – itself an influence on Smash TV.

Hidden Horses have 20 id Software alumni on the books, including former lead VFX artist Todd Boyce, principal engine programmer Dustin Land, senior AI and gameplay engineer Daniel Young, producer Andrew Willis, senior technical designer Jordan Turner, principal technical designer Tim Locke, and senior skybox artist Allison Dombek. They're looking to make "the kind of old school shooters that we think people want more of," in Land's words.

In a recent development, all members of Hidden Horses own a share of the manufacturer, with bosses "democratically" appointed, in the words of a FAQ. "Our structure is quite flat, and we elect leaders when needed," Willis told Vertical Slice in a separate interview. "Financially, this means we are not subject to investor demands and the preservation of the company and the jobs it sustains is paramount over needless growth and our 'capital' doesn't compete for returns with other potential investments.".

All of which is obviously gesturing towards the horse elephant in the room: Microsoft, who've made enormous cuts to their Xbox biz in their eagerness to further supercharge their $4 trillion market value.

Recent findings suggest that "We've replicated some things, changed some things, and added others [from our id Software days]," Willis went on. "Overall, I think top-down hierarchy is something we all have bad experiences with—we also don't want to trend chase or make a game by focus group. We want to make the kinds of classic gameplay focused games that we would play ourselves. We think there is a market for that and our experiences with the gaming community in our past work history informs that.".

Willis's hope is that the "flat" structure will motivate staff to work harder, because they feel like they have a meaningful say over the firm's direction. "It allows all ideas to be considered and means we don't miss out on any contributions from our employees just because they don't sit high up in some arbitrary hierarchy," he mentioned..

According to recent reports, I'm cynical about "flat" firm structures, myself. I think they are very often just an excuse for the biggest egos in a company to throw their weight around. It can work given a friendly initial mix of founders, but it gets complicated when you start hiring fresh people who don't have the same chemistry. Mind you, there are no intends to expand the company dramatically for the foreseeable. "We want to create a vehicle that allows us to make games for our livelihoods, not to make crazy profits and get 100x returns," Willis went on. I'm also a bit leery of the fact that Hidden Horses have popped up a Kickstarter, because I'm leery about crowd-funding in general, even when Peter Molyneux isn't involved. The studio founders are currently working on some promotional initiatives to drum up support, including a studio documentary and *squints* a promotional beer? Still, I'm happy to hear that at least a few Cacodemon wranglers jettisoned by the big M have landed on their hooves feet. I wish Hidden Horses the best of luck with it all. As for Danger Pay, proper screens, footage and release details are to follow.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mystic Messenger, arguably one of the best dating sims around, has been dormant for about seven years.
  • The free-to-play mobile dating sim has started banning players with seemingly too many Hourglasses - the game’s virtual currency - saved up in their accounts.
  • The news exploded on the Mystic Messenger subreddit overnight, with over a dozen reports from players logging in to play normally, only to receive an in-game notice that their accounts had been banned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mystic Messenger, arguably one of the best dating sims around, has been dormant for about seven years. Despite not receiving newly introduced content or any meaningful updates in all that time, the game remains popular with its core fans, many of whom just woke up to some shocking news about their accounts.

The free-to-play mobile dating sim has started banning players with seemingly too many Hourglasses - the game’s virtual currency - saved up in their accounts. So far, it looks like players with 1,000 or more have been targeted, but others with far fewer hoards have reported getting the axe, too.

The news exploded on the Mystic Messenger subreddit overnight, with over a dozen reports from players logging in to play normally, only to receive an in-game notice that their accounts had been banned.

It has been revealed that the message players received is identical, and doesn’t mention the specific reason for the ban. “Your account has been banned because abusive behavior has been detected from your account,” it reads, ending with a support email address the affected user can contact if they believe they’d banned in error.

It didn’t take a while for players to realise that most, if not all of the bans are for players with thousands of Hourglasses in their accounts. The virtual currency can both be acquired in-game just by playing, as well as through direct real-money purchases.

For a nearly ten-year-old game that stopped receiving content three years into its life, it’s easy to see how a dedicated group of players would be able to acquire so many Hourglasses by simply playing regularly for so long.

When contacted by the affected players, Cheritz, the developer and publisher of the game, has instructed them to send receipts of how they acquired Hourglasses (assuming they were purchased) to verify whether or not they’d been fraudulently obtained.

Considering that Mystic Messenger has practically been abandoned by its developer, certain exploits have emerged over the years that allowed players to farm Hourglasses faster than intended, but those instances have always been dealt with then and there.

The blanket and sudden nature of this ban is what’s spooked players, especially those who’ve been logging in for years and never thought accruing in-game currency from playing the game too much would make them the target of a ban.

The running theory is that most of the bans are unintentional, and may be the result of a fresh automated security system that’s been implemented. It’s entirely possible, especially if its’s AI-based, that the new system simply couldn’t distinguish between those who have earned (or bought) their Hourglasses fairly, and those who used exploits.

The timing of the ban wave is also suspect. With the game’s 10th anniversary coming up in July, it could be that Cheriz is preparing to release a large patch for Mystic Messenger, which may include new content. If most of the playerbase is already sitting on massive amounts of in-game currency, they may simply use that to fast-track their way to unlocking the new content, which would greatly affect the developer’s bottom line.

Industry observers note that this is a problem that other live service games have run into in the past. Just recently, extraction shooter Arc Raiders added a cap to the amount of Cred players can hold in their accounts very rapidly after its launch. That currency is used to buy cosmetic sets in the store, so the logic is easy to follow.

All of that has certainly put a damper on the enthusiasm of the game’s most active players, many of whom were excited to get together in person for the coming 10th anniversary, participate in community nights and so on to celebrate.

It’s also disheartening to see a fanbase so loyal; playing a game as regularly for so long without upcoming content, to be treated so poorly. Even without knowing what the game is, it’s impressive that so many people have kept the flag of their favourite game flying for so long.

  • It has been revealed that then, you'll need to head to Duskwood to gather the Night Watchman's Torch, a handy light source primarily used to light up areas across the darkened woods near Stormwind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft secret hunters are a noble breed, known for scouring the MMO for years for hidden trinkets and treasures. With World of Warcraft: Forever's launch, they've uncovered a quest chain for an especially fancy sword.

Sources indicate that over the past week, members of the WoW Secret Hunters Discord found a quest chain that takes place entirely on the Zephras Isle, meaning you'll need to have access to the Skyborne elves to grab this sword. Navigating the island, you'll need to first pick up an ancient heirloom ring from the starting zone. Simple enough!

It has been revealed that then, you'll need to head to Duskwood to gather the Night Watchman's Torch, a handy light source primarily used to light up areas across the darkened woods near Stormwind. It turns out this torch has uses far beyond this one zone however, as taking it back to the Ruins of Ban'aethal on the Zephras Isle will reward you with a secret quest and the Ancient Hilt.

With the hilt and ring, you then must track down an Ancient Blade from one of several spawn locations on the Zephras Isle. Once you finally track it down, that's the end of part one of this quest chain. You get the sword: Eluvi'ana, which on its own isn't particularly strong, but is speculated to be upgraded later down the line.

You then need to get a corrupted water globe from either Darkshore or the Blackfathom Deeps dungeon depending on your faction, do a fetch quest for a hidden spirit in Ashenvale, then take your hoard of special quest items to a NPC in the new Shen'Dralar zone.

Sources indicate that he won't give you the finished sword. Instead he sends you to gather more items from higher-level zones. You'll need to raid a secluded vault in Feralas that you can only see with the Ancient Hilt, dive underwater in Azshara, and kill Highborne Shades in Winterspring. Once you've done all that, you can then cleanse the orb up in Hyjal, speak to the fella back in Shen'Dralar, then shimmy over to the end game Dire Maul dungeon to speak to Prince Tortheldrin about *another* sword.

Recent findings suggest that this is how far the World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunter community has gotten to. It's believed that grinding up the Shen'dralar reputation to Honoured is required for the next step, as Prince Tortheldrin pretty much says as much in his dialogue. So the hunt is still on!

These sorts of secrets make up an key part of any good MMO: the solving of mysteries in these vast digital open worlds. In retail WoW, I have fond memories of the Waist of Time quest chain, which was an arduous and comical grind for a fancy belt during the Battle for Azeroth expansion. This secret sword quest chain may very well evolve into something as legendary as that, at least I hope so!

Sources indicate that if you're not already playing it, World of Warcraft: Forever is plenty of fun. A record-breaking number of players are making the journey through Azeroth right now, diving into quests and dungeons new and old.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The developer of cozy farming game Tiny Terraces notes their sales on Steam were roughly 148 times those on the Epic Games Store, clocking in at $136,195 on Steam and $916 on Epic for a year (pre-tax).

Recent findings suggest that solo game dev VuVuu waded into discussion of the PC gaming store wars on Twitter. "Make sure to get Gaben seven more yachts," they added, plugging the game's Steam store page. Valve co-founder Gabe Newell does love his yachts.

According to recent reports, this chatter began with a post from indie dev Evgeny Grishakov dissecting the revenue splits offered by Valve and Epic. Valve famously takes a base 30% from all Steam sales, while Epic only takes 12% but takes exactly 0% of your first $1 million gross every year. And yet, Grishakov says, "Steam is still the better deal for most indie games, because that’s where the players are." Many, many indie developers have told me the same thing over the years.

In the replies to Grishakov's post, multiple developers claim to see 0-3% of sales from Epic's store. The Hive developer Skydome agrees, "I will gladly pay Steam 30% for the visibility and revenue they bring." They note that, "For comparison, Epic made only 1.4% of our revenue compared to Steam last year.".

There's no questioning Steam's dominance. But an interesting exception to this rule has also resurfaced, and it's for a game I actually played pre-release at GDC earlier this year.

Kernel Hearts is a multiplayer 3D action roguelike about magical girls. One of those girls, the pink-haired Fernet, became a Fortnite skin, and a very popular one at that. Fernet was so popular that many people would buy Kernel Hearts through the Epic Games Store just to get the skin for Fortnite. This is where Epic's Fortnite-connected marketplace and more generous rev share can actually make an impact.

"That outfit alone is worth roughly $17USD, so anyone familiar with the Kernel Hearts brand will almost certainly find the EGS offer more appealing since a significant part of our game are the character's designs," Kernel Hearts dev Ephemera Games wrote in October.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

It has been revealed that "Roughly 6 out of every 10 copies sold across PC were on the Epic Games Store, 3 on Steam and 1 on Xbox," the studio explains. "This is a pretty unusual split, especially considering that the game is available on all storefronts at pretty much the same price.".

Recent findings suggest that now factor in the rev share and $1 million grace period. "At 100k units sold for $20, that's $2M in revenue," Ephemera begins. "On Steam, you'd pay roughly $600k in platform fees. On Epic, your first million has 0% fees, and the remaining million has a 12% cut. That's just $120k in fees, a difference of $480,000! THATS A WHOLE OTHER GAME FUNDED!!!

It has been revealed that "Of course, this is a simplified example that doesn't account for regional pricing, refunds, taxes, or other deductions," the studio admits, but neither Steam nor Epic offer a magical solution to the tax fairy. "But for a small studio like ours, that's a life-changing amount of money that can go directly into funding our future projects! So yeah! Put your game on EGS.".

Industry observers note that kernel Hearts is an outlier. Not every game has a highly marketable and fashionable magical girl to act as a Fortnite magnet. But even as a corner case, it's a perfectly valid data point that demonstrates how developers can make out better if they can somehow generate relevant sales on the Epic Games Store. Therein lies the problem. Situations like Tiny Terraces are infinitely more common due to Steam's dominance (attributable largely to Steam's user experience), and Epic does not seem to be making convincing moves to change that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CD Projekt Red have reportedly enlisted Ukrainian AI firm Respeecher to modify voice lines recorded for the Polish version of Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher 3's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion. The move's been made with the permission of Geralt's Polish voice actor, Jacek Rozenek, and is rooted in the studio wanting his upcoming lines to sound similar to the ones he recorded for the original game prior to having a stroke which has altered how he sounds.

Recent findings suggest that game File report that after suffering a stroke in 2019 and having to rehabilitate his speech, Rozenek was able to record some lines as Geralt for a quest in The Witcher 3's 2022 next-gen update, but that doing so left the actor "so exhausted". With next year's Songs of the Past expansion, CD Projekt Red were seemingly more concerned about making sure lines recorded by post-stroke Rozenek don't sound markedly different to those he recorded a decade ago for the base game and its existing expansions.

After a meeting between the two sides confirmed that Rozenek's voice had grown lower and gruffer due to some combination of the stroke and him simply getting older, the studio made the decision not to recast the actor, but instead let modify Respeecher modify his lines to make them sound closer to those original recordings. Rozenek reportedly gave his blessing for this to go ahead. "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," he told Game File. "I have great trust...for the creators of this game.".

It has been revealed that this isn't the first time CD Projekt Red have enlisted Respeecher's services. Back in 2023, it was revealed that the studio had used speech synthesis software to make ripperdoc Viktor Vektor's lines in the Polish version of Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion sound like actor Miłogost Reczek. Reczek died in 2021 before he could reprise his role as Vektor for the DLC, so rather than recasting the character across the whole game to avoid noticeable differences in voice, CD Projekt got another actor to voice Vektor's new lines for Phantom Liberty, then used the genAI tech to make those lines sound like Reczek was delivering them. CD Projekt Red said at the time that they'd gotten permission from Reczek's family before going ahead with their plan.

According to recent reports, speaking to Game File about this latest use of genAI on Rozenek's Songs of the Past lines, CD Projekt localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed noted that "as a person working with voice actors over all the regions in the world, this is a significant concern". "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good," he added. The argument the studio are making at current is that this was "a special case" due to Rozenek's specific situation with Songs of the Past.

Geralt's English voice actor Doug Cockle reportedly won't have his lines for the latest expansion get the same genAI treatment, nor will any lines Rozenek records for future Witcher games, with the studio seemingly happy to lean on the passage of in-game time as an explanation for Geralt sounding different in the latter case.

In a recent development, as ever, there's a debate to be had as to whether CD Projekt Red should have simply recast Rozenek's role in Songs of the Past if the difference bothered them so, possibly while bringing the actor on to help tutor whomever his human replacement for Songs of the Past would be in nailing the exact gravelly tone needed for Geralt. That way, you'd have two actors being paid for work rather than forking out for genAI instead of one of them, though it's possibly an idea that'd only work well in theory. If I were Rozenek I'm not sure I'd be totally happy aiding someone who could potentially be tapped to replace me going forwards, though it does very much seem like the lesser of two evils when compared to the potential of voice actors being replaced by genAI line readings.

In a recent development, as far as the game alone is concerned, I'm also not sure Geralt's voice being different in the new expansion is something that'd bother me too much when playing. One would assume he'd not suddenly be sounding like a member of Alvin and the Chipmunks, and there are plenty of storyline justifications you could concoct or lean on for him sounding that bit gruffer at times.

The anticipated sequel in the open-world driving game series doesn’t officially launch until May 19, but owners of its most expensive version - the Premium Edition - can play it right now.

Sources indicate that that version of the game includes more than just a few days of early access, of course, but you’d think the $120 price tag would’ve only been palatable to a small group of players. Not the case with this game.

Sources indicate that forza Horizon 6, which has spent 16 weeks in Steam’s global top sellers list, currently occupies the number two spot, having jumped up three spots this week in anticipation of the launch. The game has also naturally been popular with players, so popular in fact that it has already overtaken the player counts of all other Horizon games on the platform.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, the game has peaked at 128,157 concurrent players on Steam alone (via SteamDB). The figure has already climbed several times during the writing of this story, so you can only imagine how much higher it’s going to get deeper into the weekend.

In a recent development, all of that, of course, days before the official launch on Tuesday, when, theoretically, the majority of the game’s audience will be able to start playing. In just a few short hours, Horizon 6 has already gone well above Forza Horizon 5’s peak concurrent of 81,096, as well as Forza Horizon 4’s peak 75,689 players.

It has been revealed that steam is the only platform that publishes player numbers, of course, but it’s easy to see how similar the enthusiasm is going to be on Xbox. Though the game is not yet part of the Game Pass line-up, those who don’t want to wait could buy the Premium Edition Upgrade to get the included content, and play it right now.

Sources indicate that game Pass, and Xbox / Windows Store numbers don’t factor into Steam’s, which is another thing to consider when viewing the numbers holistically. Indeed, given how successful Forza Horizon 5 has been on PlayStation 5, Horizon 6’s upcoming release on Sony's console is bound to be even bigger.

Forza Horizon 5 has been off to a similarly flying start in the first few days of its own advanced access launch, so it’s obviously not surprising to see Horizon 6 do better there. In case you missed it, check out our review of Forza Horizon 6. In short, we really liked it, even if we expected more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remember how stealing a cop car in the older GTA games used to get you a free shotgun? Well, turns out Vice City's police force is even better armed. If you need some extra guns rapidly, particularly shotguns and assault rifles, filching them from the trunk of a police car is a great method, though obviously it comes with certain risks.

It has been revealed that you might have realised, but stealing cars in GTA 6 is significantly more complicated than previous games, especially if they're alarmed. Thankfully, this doesn't apply to any police pickup trucks like the Bravado Bison the cops sometimes use, which you'll spot occasionally both in rural areas and in the city.

With the police pickups, you can simply climb onto the bed at the back and open the storage crate, grabbing any weapons and ammo inside, including other potential items like Stun Guns, without setting off any alarms.

In a recent development, for proper police cruisers, though, their trunks are alarmed along with the doors, meaning you'll need a tool to deal with them, the slim jim, which you get during the "Moses" mission in Chapter 2. If you slim jim the door of the cop car and get inside, the trunk will unlock, so you can head around the back, interact to open it, and steal whatever's in the boot without tackling the alarm, whether it be an assault rifle, shotgun, or even body armor.

If you don't have the slim jim yet, you can still open the trunk (you'll see your character use a screwdriver) but the alarm will go off.

Sources indicate that once you've collected the weapons, you can interact with your own car trunk, and you'll see a prompt to stow the weapons inside. You'll be rather conspicuous wandering around with an assault rifle in your hands or strapped to your back, after all.

Obviously, it's best not to try and steal cop cars with cops in them, but you can find them around, or parked at police stations, such as in Port Gellhorn or Vice City.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that playStation 5 has officially surpassed 100m consoles sold, Sony's updated sales data revealed.
  • In a recent development, the figure represents 'sell-in' units, meaning those shipped to retailers, as opposed to 'sell-through' which tracks consoles actually sold to consumers.
  • According to recent reports, nevertheless, this is an impressive achievement, and gets the PS5 ever closer to the PS4's 117m, which it achieved by June 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that playStation 5 has officially surpassed 100m consoles sold, Sony's updated sales data revealed. The milestone was reached on 10th November, almost exactly six years on from the console's launch.

In a recent development, the figure represents 'sell-in' units, meaning those shipped to retailers, as opposed to 'sell-through' which tracks consoles actually sold to consumers. In other words, the number of PS5s in people's homes is smaller than that 100m.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, this is an impressive achievement, and gets the PS5 ever closer to the PS4's 117m, which it achieved by June 2022. It also means the PS5 has almost matched the original PlayStation in units sold (102.4m). As impressive as the numbers are, historical data indicates that PS5 sales have been in decline.

Sources indicate that sony hasn't shied away from discussing that fact in its earnings reports. 2.6m PS5 consoles were sold during the most recent quarter (Q2 of FY2026), well below the 4m sold over the same period the year prior. In fact, Q2 of FY2026 is the lowest second quarter on record in terms of units sold since the PS5's launch.

However, it's also worth noting that, small though it may be, the second quarter's result is higher than the first quarter's 1.6m, the second-lowest of any single quarter since the PS5's launch, beaten only by Q4 of FY2025's 1.5m.

Sources indicate that if numbers don't recover in the third and fourth quarters, this may be the PS5's lowest year ever in terms of units sold. Although the second quarter's sales boost can be attributed to the high anticipation of Grand Theft Auto 6, the overall downturn is largely due to the console's higher price; Sony raised the PS5 and PS5 Pro's prices on several occasions since 2020. The firm's bottom line, however, hasn't been affected much, as its initiative to generate more revenue from its already-engaged audience continues to work.

#4775. Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2105 w)

Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while.
  • Instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news.
  • In a recent development, also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while. But I come back to you now at the turn of the technological tide. Well, sort of. Sadly I'm not here to predict an end to the ridiculous AI-fuelled chip crisis. That whole mess has a couple of years to run, surely.

Instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news. In short, have you seen how cheap PC gaming monitors are? I mean remarkably, almost stupendously, cheap. I'm talking £60 / $60 for an entry-level 1080p panel with triple-digit refresh rate, sub-£200 / $250 for high-refresh 4K gaming. Heck, even OLED monitors now start with a "2" in both currencies.

In a recent development, also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years. A 4K panel bought today for £200 is equivalent to paying roughly £150 back in 2020. All the while, that same £200 / $200 right now won't buy you a current-model gaming graphics card at all, even the most feeble example, and will barely secure a basic dual-channel 16GB DDR5 memory kit. Youch.

It has been revealed that so, I think we can all agree monitors are cheap in the current chip-catastrophe context. The immediate question is why? The answer isn't all that complicated, actually. Most obviously, the display market isn't being devoured by the AI craze. All those data centres are stuffed with GPUs, memory chips and NAND flash, not monitors.

By way of example, one of the largest new AI data centres on Earth is Microsoft's new Fairwater site in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin. It's thought to pack hundreds of thousands of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The cost doesn't bear thinking about, but those GPUs are built into what's known as "headless" server racks. In other words, they have no screens at all. Ultimately, the key compute hardware is all managed remotely, in which capacity the Fairwater facility is reported to presently have around 375 employees. If we generously assume each has two PC monitors, that's only 750 for the entire site.

In a recent development, AI isn't really driving demand on the end-user side of the equation, either. Put it this way: you don't need to buy a latest phone, laptop or PC to access the latest models. At the same time, the display market is suffering from something of a glut of overcapacity. Chinese companies built out huge capacity in LCD panel manufacturing over the past decade, to the extent factories are now running underutilised. Meanwhile, even the OLED market is arguably oversupplied.

In fact, Samsung and LG, the two massive noises in large OLED panel manufacturing (as opposed to OLED displays for tablets and phones), have been shifting emphasis away from TV panels to PC monitors because the latter offer better margins. Meanwhile, the AI boom has almost definitely meant lower demand for latest PCs. Certainly, the big research houses point to cratering PC sales thanks to higher component costs. Long story short, that's oodles of capacity combined with weakening demand. Like I said, the explanation for cheap monitors isn't exactly rocket surgery, if you know what I mean.

What is a bit more complicated is making sense of what's available today in the gaming monitor market. With so much choice, where exactly is the very best value to be found? And are there any remaining pain points?

It has been revealed that monitor specifications, to be sure, can be tricksy at the best of times. But if you're looking for some blanket rules to fling casually over the whole LCD monitor market - I'll be digging deeper into OLED tech another day - try these for size. Look for, at minimum, 300 nits brightness and 1ms response times. Refresh rates are a slightly more complicated call, but for the vast majority of games, 144Hz is plenty. For "esports-grade multiplayer fare like Counter-Strike or Dota 2, or I think a refresh in the high 200s will get the job done for most. If you'll benefit from more than that, you almost certainly know who you are already.

Oh, and heavily favour IPS over VA panels. Exceptions exist: there are some decent "Rapid VA" panels these days and Samsung, in particular, does some nippy VA models. But a lot of the cheaper stuff is pretty slow and smeary, making VA a risky buy. Finally, don't worry too much about claimed HDR capability, save for the fact that HDR 400 certification at least means the monitor can do 400 nits. Unless a monitor has local dimming, it won't be truly HDR capable.

Recent findings suggest that anywho, one immediate and rather ironic glitch is the growing mismatch between monitors and GPUs. For sure, it's great you can grab a high-refresh 4K monitor for such little money. It's almost hard to believe that you can have this 27-inch IPS MSI for sub-£200 (you're looking at $250 for the same model in the US), and it even has a 288Hz 1080p dual mode.

In a recent development, I actually favour 32 inches with my 4K gaming, and that's naturally a little pricier, especially if you insist on an IPS - which again, you probably should. But even $350 for that kind of panel (here's a comparable model for £340 in the UK) is a fraction of what you'd have paid for a similarly specced model a few years ago. And it probably wouldn't have included dual-mode functionality.

Here's the problem, though. How are you going to drive the thing, what with its eight million-plus pixels? After all, the cheapest RTX 5090 on Newegg right now is over $6,500. So high-end Nvidia GPUs now cost about as much as a decent used car.

Sources indicate that of course, you might be surprised just how effective the likes of an AMD RX 9070 XT or Nvidia RTX 5070-class GPU is at 4K thanks to upscaling technologies including DLSS and FSR. The latest transformer model upscalers really do knock out pretty stellar image quality. Add in a bit of frame gen and you have a compelling combination of visual sharpness, reasonably low latency and nice smoothframe rates, even in the most demanding of games. Perhaps the one thing you can't do is enable full path tracing in a game like Cyberpunk 2077 and still expect a slick experience, but standard ray tracing remains an option.

Sources indicate that the bigger snag, unsurprisingly, is that you can no longer bag a 5070 at (let alone below) its original £539 / $549 MSRP. Instead, you're looking at the thick end of £800 / $900. That's a bit of an ask for pairing with a £200 monitor, isn't it?

It has been revealed that I'd therefore argue that, for pure gaming purposes, the bang-for-buck sweet spot remains just where it's been sat twiddling its thumbs for the better part of a decade, namely 1440p. That applies to both its vanilla 16:9 aspect variety and my personally preferred ultrawide format, the latter being so very immersive and also pretty nifty for daily multi-tasking. Indeed, the 27-inch 1440p segment even brings the vibrant colours and infinite contrast of OLED panels into a reasonably affordable window.

By way of example, £179 (or $150) is enough for a circa 200Hz, IPS 1440p panel with super low (by IPS standards) pixel response, even if the 250-nit brightness is lower than I'd like. Meanwhile, as I write these words, pricing for massive-brand 27-inch 1440p gaming OLEDs kicks off at about £290 in the UK and roughly $270 in the US. Admittedly, those entry-level OLEDs come with some compromises, which I'll cover in a forthcoming post. But what you might call 'proper' OLED panels can be had around the low £300 / $300 mark - not throw-away money, for sure, but relatively accessible.

Industry observers note that the 34-inch 1440p ultrawide segment is a bit trickier, however. The good news is that conventional LCD models can be had for relative peanuts, with prices starting at about £220 or $249 for game-focused, high-refresh models. But those two example both use a VA panel, which usually means inferior pixel response.

IPS models are a little thin on the ground when it comes to 34-inch ultrawide, but sneaking in below £300 / $300 is generally possible. The real bummer is OLED, where going ultrawide invokes a massive premium. The best price I can find on a massive-brand 34-inch ultrawide today is $629 for this Asus model in the US and £648 for this MSI option in the UK.

Sources indicate that that's awfully toppy, especially when you consider that you can grab a 49-inch, 5,120x1,440 ultrawide OLED for barely any more money. I do actually quite like those 49-inch ultrawides, but I have to concede the ergonomics are challenging. However, 4K OLEDs in 27-inch and 32-inch formats can also be had for as much as £100 / $100 less than the current cheapest 34-inch 1440p ultrawides, which doesn't make much sense to me.

Recent findings suggest that again, with 4K, there's the challenge of keeping all those pixels updated. If you already have a sufficiently mighty graphics card, though, I a 32-inch 4K OLED can make a fantastic all-round option, and something like this MSI model for £549 would be absolutely lovely. You get good pixel density and lots of space for daily desktopping, plus OLED visuals and a large enough panel to be really get you into your games.

It's just a pity that 34-inch OLED ultrawides remain so weirdly expensive, it being a format that ticks so many different boxes. As for my own personal money-no-object pick, well, I'm typing these words on the new Alienware AW3926QW, the 39-inch 5K2K beast with a Tandem WOLED panel and RGB subpixels.

One could argue it's a relative steal at £1,079 or $1,100. I mean, it's pretty much peak current PC gaming display technology, and it's about half the price of what Nvidia's second-tier RTX 5080 graphics card is going for lately. Assuming you can even find one in stock.

At this point, the one major category I haven't covered is LCD monitors with mini-LED full-array local dimming. Cards on the table, I'm not a huge fan of mini-LED monitors. The detailed reasons for that are, perhaps, the subject for another day. But I've reviewed countless models and have yet to see one that didn't come with pretty serious compromises.

In a recent development, that said, the technology has gotten a lot more accessible in the last 12 to 18 months, to the extent that 27-inch 1440p models start at just over $250. I've had that specific model in and came away pretty impressed. It's very, very punchy, and even factoring in the limitations of mini-LED versus OLED when it comes to lighting control and speed, I cannot deny the temptation.

Sources indicate that just for completeness, one further exception to the general rule of cheap gaming monitors involves ultra-high refresh monitors aimed at serious esports aficionados. I'm talking about panels like this 1,000Hz LG I sampled elsewhere. At £800 / $1,000 for a 25-inch 1080p IPS panel it's inevitably a niche proposition, and poor value by normal standards.

It has been revealed that I think a much better compromise for just about everyone, short of an actual esports pro, is to grab a larger, higher resolution monitor that offers one of those windowed 1080p modes running at about 500Hz or thereabouts. That way you've got a nice high-res panel for both work and play, as well as that ultra-low latency mode for when you want to dance around Dust 2 doling out the headshots or whatever.

Industry observers note that incidentally, I realise I've gone in a bit hot and heavy with the OLED content here, the implicit assumption being OLED is all that, and notably without addressing the obvious objections like the risk of burn-in. But all that, I hope you'll be pleased to hear, is very much the subject for my next RPS post on all things OLED.

In a recent development, until then, all I can say is thank goodness PC monitors provide relative respite from the parlous state of much of the rest of the PC component market. It's absolutely brutal out there if you're building a gaming PC, but at least you'll get a lot of screen for your money.

Just to round things out, if anyone has any specific queries at any given price point, form factor or panel type, shout out below and I'll try to steer you in the direction of a decent model.

Original Story: We've already talked a little bit about the Fresh Zealand trick and how it's pretty much the number one topic on social media when it comes to Xbox and GTA 6 right now, so it's naive to think nobody's going to try it this Wednesday.

If you're not in the loop, this refers to people changing their region on Xbox to access GTA 6 at local midnight time in Latest Zealand, which equates to 6am EST / 11am GMT on Wednesday, November 18th.

Over the past couple of days, there's been a ton of debate online about whether it's "OK" or "safe" to switch regions in order to play GTA 6 early on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, and if you listen to what the majority say, the answer is that Xbox "don't care" if you do it, and that it's happened on many occasions without bans in the past.

However, it's true that Xbox specifically states in its TOCs that you shouldn't change regions unless you've actually moved to the country in question, and over on X/Twitter today, Windows Central editor Jez Corden and YouTuber Colt Eastwood revealed that they talked about this exact topic during a recent visit to Xbox's headquarters in Seattle.

Here's what they had to say about it in response to another of WC's writers (apologies for the profanity in the tweet!):.

A lot of people still believe that the risk is extremely low though, with some even arguing that it's "fear mongering" to suggest that Xbox will start suspending or banning people for wanting to play GTA 6 a few hours early.

There are others in the industry, such as The Verge editor Tom Warren, who also believe it's a non-problem:.

The reality is that nobody knows for sure whether Xbox will take action against people switching their consoles to Newly introduced Zealand to play GTA 6 early this Wednesday, but based on historical evidence, it seems pretty unlikely.

Is it worth taking the risk though? That's the bit we'll leave up to you, and speaking personally, I would never want to recommend doing something like this in case Microsoft suddenly decides to throw the ban hammer around.

Let's wait and see how it all pans out on Wednesday, eh?

Are you using the Newly introduced Zealand trick for GTA 6? Are you worried about the risks? Tell us below.

💡 Key Takeaways
